newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Japan moves to boost drive for finservices pact.
newsitem.headline: Japan moves to boost drive for finservices pact.

text.p: Japan offered on Friday to permanently lift curbs on foreign companies operating in its financial services market in what it called a bid to raise prospects for a global pact in the booming sector.

The offer, together with another by Switzerland, was lodged with the World Trade Organisation (WTO) on the eve of a new round of talks next week to assess prospects for a deal among the body's 131 members by the year-end deadline.
"Japan strongly hopes that our initiative will be echoed by other (WTO) members," Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said in a statement distributed in Tokyo and Geneva.

The offer, based on a package of Japanese financial reforms unveiled last month, provides for removal of control on foreign exchange and allow firms and individuals to deal directly with overseas banks and brokers.
It would also permit foreign insurance firms to offer services in Japan without opening offices in the country, and to enter the insurance broking business.

If other key countries came up with similar "meaningful improvements" of their current offers, the Japanese statement suggested, this would be a major contribution "to the successful conclusion of the talks."

Japan is the second of the four top trading powers -- the others are the United States, the European Union and Canada -- to table a fresh offer before a target date of July 14 set when the negotiations were launched earlier this year.

The talks mark the second attempt to get a financial services pact since an effort tied to other trading sectors in the 1986-93 Uruguay Round negotiations was dropped to avoid blocking an overall global trade treaty, signed in 1994.

The first attempt since then almost collapsed when the United States walked out in June 1995, arguing that offers from key emerging economies were not enough to justify it pledging to open its own market, the world's biggest, to all comers.

Under EU pressure, an interim deal was shaped involving Japan, Canada and many other developed and developing countries. But that runs out at the end of this year and there is no support for renewal without U.S. participation.
The United States and Canada promised in June that they would have their own new offers in by next Tuesday.

But a senior U.S. official said at the time that leading Asian and Latin American countries would have to pledge to lift a range of current restrictions on foreign firms in the financial services sector before Washington could sign up to a global deal.

That warning was echoed on Friday by EU Commissioner for financial services Mario Monti, who told reporters that the 15-nation bloc would also walk away from a pact if liberalisation offered by other countries was insufficient.

In remarks in Brussels resembling those of Mitsuzuka, Monti appealed to other powers to match the EU offer. "The WTO financial services negotiations are the most important item on the world trade agenda this year," he declared.
EU trade officials told journalists in Brussels later that a return to bilateral agreements on opening financial services -- or retreat from a global deal under the WTO, would be a setback.
"Experience has shown that a rules-based, transparent system is clearly the best way ahead," one said.
